A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MLSAE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V2 reports original MLSAE training and evaluation results, including reconstruction errors, downstream losses, activation heatmaps, variance ratios, and hyperparameter analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds directly trained single-layer comparisons, additional transformer evaluations, and synthetic-control and alternative-metric analyses.

M1.justification: The shared TopK architecture, AuxK component, and tuned-lens procedure are retained. However, Equation 3 replaces an explicit average of layer-specific FVU ratios with an unindexed FVU ratio. The PDFs do not clearly establish whether this merely states the loss per input or changes its aggregation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the Pile excluding Books3 and the same illustrative indirect-object-identification prompt for residual-stream analysis. Added transformer configurations and analysis controls do not introduce another text corpus, language, or application task.

E2.justification: V2 compares MLSAE performance with published single-layer results. V3 additionally trains single-layer SAEs on Pythia-70m, 160m, and 410m and evaluates them directly against MLSAEs, including a tuned-lens Pythia-70m comparison (Appendix B.4, Figures 19–22). This substantially strengthens the comparator design.

E3.justification: V3 adds MLSAE configurations for Pythia-1.4b, Gemma 2 2B, Llama 3.2 3B, and GPT-2 small. The new Gemma experiment uses approximately 2.5 billion training tokens versus the usual billion. Additional protocols include train-layer/test-layer comparisons excluding the final layer, Gaussian reference controls, threshold-based active-layer counts, and normalized entropy.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained hyperparameter and tuned-lens analyses, v3 investigates cross-layer transfer of single-layer SAEs, possible duplicated latents using synthetic controls, sensitivity to heatmap normalization, and alternative measures of multi-layer activity (Appendices B.4, B.6, and C). These test substantial new questions about the central findings.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains the same mean-and-standard-deviation reporting across decoder-vector similarities, with additional model rows. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the new reference histograms are supplementary analyses rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial model, baseline, and supplementary results. For example, Table 1 newly reports Gemma 2 2B FVU 0.210 and delta cross-entropy 1.483; retained Pythia FVU and cross-entropy entries are unchanged. The expanded-model summary changes single-token variance fractions from about 1% to roughly 1–10%. Table 1 also removes its MSE and KL summary entries, although these metrics remain in other plots.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a counterexample showing that more active layers need not imply greater layer-index variance, and defines alternative threshold-count and normalized-entropy measures with entropy bounds. The existing law-of-total-variance analysis remains substantively unchanged; no substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: a shared multi-layer SAE, contrasting aggregate and single-token activity, model-size trends, and qualitatively similar findings with tuned lenses. New experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands qualifications surrounding the central interpretation. Appendix C explains information discarded by normalization, the ordinal-layer assumption, and threshold dependence, while alternative metrics expose differing expansion-factor trends. Appendix B additionally discusses duplicated latents as an alternative explanation, slower Gemma convergence, and the rationale for excluding final-layer comparisons.

D1.justification: V3 adds GPU types and training durations, explicitly describes balanced layer stacking within batches, and supplies additional tuned-lens source and released-model access information. The existing optimizer, preprocessing, principal hyperparameters, and code-access disclosure are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Llama 3, elaborates the ICA/SAE relationship, and changes its description of Yun et al. from an undercomplete basis to a sparse dictionary. The principal novelty positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained with localized clarifications. V3 introduces an evaluation subsection, reorganizes and expands Appendices B and C, and adds acknowledgements and a reproducibility statement. This is limited restructuring rather than extensive rewriting of existing prose.

P2.justification: Table 1 is transposed, expanded, and moved into the main text. Existing figures gain model entries or move, including the hyperparameter variance plot becoming Figure 27. Numerous new comparison matrices, control histograms, heatmaps, and metric panels substantially expand the visual presentation; Appendix D heatmaps are retained.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens a central weakness of v2: its claim of comparable single-layer performance now has directly trained baseline evidence instead of relying on literature comparisons. Architecture checks and tests of duplicated latents, normalization, and metric choice also improve the empirical foundation. Final-layer exclusion limits the baseline conclusions, and the written FVU aggregation remains ambiguous, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
